failure_modes.description: Queue length is a poor proxy for traffic demand when considering downstream capacity constraints
failure_modes.evidence: Traffic flow theory shows that queue length doesn't distinguish between demand and supply constraints. A long queue may indicate insufficient downstream capacity rather than high demand, leading to misallocation of green time.

failure_modes.description: Network signal coordination requires explicit timing plans to prevent platoon dispersion
failure_modes.evidence: Decades of traffic engineering research demonstrate that uncoordinated local optimization leads to platoon dispersion and increased delays. The TRANSYT and SCOOT algorithms were developed specifically to address this limitation.

failure_modes.description: The mechanism fails to account for pedestrian and cross-street traffic patterns
failure_modes.evidence: Queue-based optimization prioritizes vehicle throughput while ignoring pedestrian crossing requirements, which often have fixed minimum timing needs that cannot be dynamically reduced without creating safety hazards.

failure_modes.description: Similar adaptive signal control systems have been extensively studied and deployed
failure_modes.evidence: SCATS, SCOOT, and RHODES systems all implement network-wide adaptive signal control with proven effectiveness. The proposed mechanism represents only marginal variation on these established approaches.

failure_modes.description: The hypothesis predicts increased average travel time when tested in realistic network conditions
failure_modes.evidence: Microsimulation studies consistently show that uncoordinated local optimization increases network-wide travel times by 15-30% compared to properly coordinated systems, directly contradicting the hypothesis.

failure_modes.description: The mechanism cannot achieve network-wide optimization objectives
failure_modes.evidence: Network traffic optimization requires global objectives (like total person throughput) that cannot be achieved through purely local decisions. Individual intersection optimization leads to suboptimal network performance.
